book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan
book.volume: Volume X of The Operating Discipline for AI Library

name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health
blurb: In a small study in Turkey, one class of sixth graders took a visual arts course that used AI tools, while a similar class took the same course without them. By the end, the students who used AI held more positive attitudes toward art and scored higher on the course outcomes (Kara, 2025).
title: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

papers.title: Innovations of music and aesthetic education courses using intelligent technologies
papers.caveat: Music schools, not general classrooms; no randomized control.
papers.finding: 343 elementary, middle, and high school students in Beijing music schools improved instrument proficiency with intelligent technologies; gains varied by instrument.

papers.why: Only K-12 visual arts study found.
papers.title: The Effect of Artificial Intelligence Applications in 6th Grade Visual Arts Course on Student Attitudes and Course Outcomes
papers.venue: International Journal of Modern Education Studies
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment with 40 sixth graders in Turkey: AI-supported visual arts lessons raised attitudes and course outcome scores over a control group.

papers.why: Only review found for AI in PE.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Physical Education: A Systematic Review of Personalized Learning, Assessment, and Performance Analytics
papers.caveat: Mixed K-12 and higher ed; low-profile journal; mostly short studies.
papers.finding: Review of 87 studies (K-12 and higher education): AI in PE linked to engagement and more consistent assessment; concerns about data privacy, bias, and weak teacher-AI frameworks.

children.name: The Authorship Rule
children.blurb: The Authorship Rule is a school-wide agreement that students must make their own creative work and disclose any AI help they use.

children.name: Music Practice and Composition
children.blurb: AI can support music practice and composition by providing accompaniment tracks, generating theory drills, and offering feedback on student work, but it must not replace the student's own creative choices or the teacher's role as the primary source of feedback.

children.name: Art History and Portfolios
children.blurb: AI can help art teachers open conversations about artworks and help students reflect on their portfolios, while the student keeps the final say on selection and reflection.

children.name: Drama and Performance
children.blurb: AI can serve drama and performance in two ways: as a rehearsal partner that reads scene lines so a student can practice timing, memorization, and delivery at home, and as a drafting aid for the production's administrative work, such as rehearsal schedules, prop lists, and program notes.

children.name: Physical Education: Planning and Adaptation
children.blurb: AI can help physical education teachers build banks of adapted activities, station rotations, and personal fitness plans, saving planning time so more time goes to teaching.

children.name: Form Feedback From Video
children.blurb: Form feedback from video means students record their own movement, such as a basketball shot or a running stride, and watch it back to compare with good form, sometimes with AI tools that analyze the movement and suggest improvements.

children.name: Health Education
children.blurb: A school configured health education tool lets students ask health questions anonymously and get answers drawn only from materials the school nurse and health teacher have approved.

children.name: Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools
children.blurb: Student health information is among the most sensitive data a school holds, and typing a diagnosis, medication, or injury into a general AI chat tool shares that record with a company the school has no agreement with.

children.name: Teaching Students About AI Art
children.blurb: Teaching students about AI art means using the arts classroom to examine images, music, and video made by machines, and to ask what human creators contribute that a generator does not.

children.name: Media Arts, Photography, and Film
children.blurb: Media arts, photography, and film classes already use digital tools with built-in AI features, such as photo editors that remove objects or change backgrounds and video editors that generate captions or suggest cuts.

children.name: Arts and PE for Students With Disabilities
children.blurb: AI tools can open arts and physical education to students with disabilities by offering new ways to create and move, such as voice commands, eye tracking, or audio feedback for music.

children.name: Planning and Feedback for Arts and PE Teachers
children.blurb: AI can serve as a planning partner for arts, music, PE, and health teachers who often work alone in their buildings, helping them generate lesson ideas and draft family communications.

sections.body: This part of school life covers arts, music, physical education, and health, the subjects where the student's own hands, voice, and body are the point. The book describes AI here as a brainstorm partner, a practice aid, and a planning tool for teachers, never the maker of student work. A painting made by a machine is not a student's painting, and a fitness plan does nothing unless the student moves. The research base is thinner than in reading or math, and most ideas are sensible practices rather than proven methods. A small study of sixth graders in Turkey found that a visual arts class using AI tools held more positive attitudes toward art and scored higher on course outcomes, though with only 40 students at one school it proves little on its own.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI can play a useful role even in the most human of subjects, and a review of 87 studies of AI in physical education linked it to better engagement and more consistent assessment. It also reports real concerns about privacy and bias, and notes that existing studies are small and mostly not randomized, so teachers should treat these ideas as worth trying carefully, not as sure bets. The rule the book holds to is simple: AI can be a brainstorm partner, a practice aid, and a planning tool, but it is never the maker of student work. The common failure pattern is the generated masterpiece, where a student submits a striking image or song made entirely by AI and the teacher either misses it or has no rule to point to, after which other students follow and the program ends up grading machine work.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the authorship rule outward into each subject and then into the safeguards. The Authorship Rule and Teaching Students About AI Art set the line for creative work, while Music Practice and Composition, Art History and Portfolios, Drama and Performance, Media Arts, Photography, and Film, and Arts and PE for Students With Disabilities show how that line applies across different kinds of student making. Physical Education: Planning and Adaptation and Form Feedback From Video cover how AI supports planning and feedback without replacing the student's movement, and Planning and Feedback for Arts and PE Teachers gathers the teacher-facing side. Health Education and Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools close the section with the special care student health information requires, including testing crisis routing before any student sees a health question tool. A teacher would go to the authorship and subject pages for classroom practice, a leader to the health and privacy pages for district rules, and a parent to the authorship rule to understand where the line sits for their child's work.
